definition.value: A share-volume-based turnover measure: each stock's average monthly number of shares traded over the prior three months, scaled by its shares outstanding and expressed as a percentage.

evidence.quote: We measure the turnover rate of every stock in the following way. For every month t, we calculate the average monthly trading volume (the average number of shares traded during the previous three months, i.e., during months t-3, t-2 and t-1) and divide it by the number of shares outstanding of that firm. We then express this ratio as a percentage to obtain our turnover rate variable.

economic_intuition.value: Number of shares traded relative to shares outstanding is used as a tractable, CRSP-derived proxy for a stock's expected holding period; by Amihud and Mendelson's (1986) equilibrium result that returns rise with expected holding period, returns should fall with this share-volume-based turnover measure.

evidence.location: Section 2, Turnover rate, liquidity and asset returns (p.206)
evidence.quote: Since A&M's model implies that the observed (gross) asset return must be an increasing function of the expected holding periods, it also implies that the observed asset return must be a decreasing function of the turnover rate of that asset.
the data on turnover rates is relatively easy to obtain (it can be constructed from the CRSP tapes on a monthly basis)
evidence.interpretation: Motivates share volume / shares outstanding specifically because both series are directly available on CRSP, unlike the bid-ask spread used by prior studies.

evidence.quote: we find that the stock returns are strongly negatively related to their turnover rates confirming the notion that illiquid stocks provide higher average returns

evidence.quote: A slope coefficient of 4.5 basis points per month implies that in our sample the illiquid stocks earned a higher return of 27 basis points per month or about 3.25% per annum as compared to the liquid stocks.

we subtracted the turnover rate of an illiquid stock (the 10th percentile) from that of a liquid stock (the 90th percentile) and found the difference to be around 6%. A slope coefficient of 4.5 basis points per month implies that in our sample the illiquid stocks earned a higher return of 27 basis points per month or about 3.25% per annum as compared to the liquid stocks.
evidence.interpretation: A prose-stated economic magnitude (not a single table cell): the ~-0.045%-per-month average slope across Table 2 specifications, applied to a ~6-percentage-point gap in turnover between 10th- and 90th-percentile stocks.

notes: Derived independently, directly from the paper's full text (data/paper_text_cache/Liquidity and stock returns- An alternative test.pdf.txt) -- Sections 2 (theoretical motivation), 3 (Litzenberger-Ramaswamy/Fama-MacBeth GLS methodology), 4 (data/turnover construction), and 5 (Table 2 results and the illiquidity-premium magnitude), plus Table 2 itself. Not derived from, or checked against, the LLM raw extraction already sitting in runs/method_specs/raw/; this file exists specifically to be an independent ground truth against which that (or any future) extraction can be scored. The paper has only one liquidity signal -- CRSP shares-traded scaled by shares outstanding -- so the content here is necessarily close to the companion 'turnover' target file in this same Eval directory; both were written independently from the paper text under this target's own name ('ShareVol'), not copied from one another or from the raw extraction. Construction is a Litzenberger-Ramaswamy/Fama-MacBeth-style GLS-pooled monthly cross-sectional regression slope, not a sorted long-short portfolio, so sorts/legs are intentionally empty. Primary result is the complete-dataset univariate slope (Table 2, Panel A, first row, -0.04, t=-8.86); the full-control and trimmed-dataset rows are secondary/robustness metrics, and the 27-bps/month implied illiquidity premium is a directly quoted, prose-stated economic magnitude.
